s16.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:05 AM · THE WHARF → THE 101 NORTH
body: The Wharf Rat’s sign has said WHARF RAT in pink neon since before Jack was born, and these days only the RAT holds steady; the WHARF comes and goes. Past it the boards run on another hundred feet over the black water, past the bait shack and the fish-cleaning sink, out beyond the last of the light from the Anchor’s windows, and down at the very end a car is idling with its top up and one taillight laying a little red on the planks.

Jack comes down the wharf at five past one with his apron stuffed in his back pocket, his hands still pruned from eight hours of the Hobart, and Gloria’s white box held out in front of him by the string so nothing inside it shifts. He can hear the tape deck before he gets there — Stevie Nicks at a murmur through the canvas, the same side of the same album. Before he reaches the car she leans across from the driver’s seat and shoves his door open from inside.
“Coat check,” she says.

She has on a different flannel, green and black and big enough for two of her, and nothing at all on her feet. He gets in with the box on his knees and watches her find the clutch barefoot. She looks tired around the eyes in a way she didn’t on Friday, and wide awake everywhere else.
“How was work?”

“Work,” she says, and becomes it. She plucks three pins out of the corner of her mouth that aren’t there, sets them back between her teeth, and talks around them from somewhere in the old country by way of Burbank — “Arms up. Down. You ate a sandwich since Thursday, I can tell, I am not angry, I am only telling you” — and then she’s the girl inside the dress, standing very still on a box with her chin up, apologizing to a hem. Back and forth, the woman and the girl, until the woman gets the last pin in and the girl says “Ow” in a very small voice. Then the pins go back wherever she keeps them.
“Since ten this morning,” she says, as herself. “I drove up after. I’ve been back two hours. I took a shower and lay on the floor.” She glances down at his lap. “What’s in the box?”
“My grandmother’s pie.”

Her eyes stay on the box a little longer — the white cardboard, Gloria’s red-and-white string knotted twice — and he watches her decide to come back to it. She puts the car in gear and rolls them up the wharf with the headlights off until they’re past the Anchor’s windows.
“Not the diner you work at,” she says. “I’m not eating pie in front of your boss.”
He told her about the Anchor at Ellery, somewhere in the two hours in the Saab — Gloria and the pie ratings, the Hobart, which end of the wharf. Apparently she kept all of it.

Mission Street is dark from the water to the freeway. At the on-ramp the all-night place sits under its own tall sign with every window blazing, a yellow box with a cop at the counter and three cars out front and a busboy mopping in the middle of all that light. Skye slows, and looks at it, and doesn’t turn in.
“Too bright,” she says, and takes the ramp north.
Jack met her in the one dark corner of a glass house and spent the rest of that night on a beach lit by oil platforms. He figures she likes the dark end of things. He figures he can live with it.
“Where, then?”
“Twenty minutes. Somewhere nobody I know has ever been.”

The 101 runs along the water for a few miles past the last of the town, the sea on their left darker than the sky and the railroad keeping it company, and then the highway turns its back on the ocean and starts to climb, up through a cut in the hills where the dark gets bigger and the trucks get slower, their running lights strung up the grade ahead of them like beads off a broken rosary.

s17.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:30 AM · THE STARLITE, A TRUCK STOP ON THE 101
body: The Starlite smells of coffee that has been on the burner since the last shift change, diesel off the islands, and something sugary going dark on a griddle. It sits at the top of the grade, where the trucks pull off to breathe: six diesel islands under sodium lamps the color of weak tea, a gravel apron where the eighteen-wheelers park nose to tail and idle in their sleep, and a long low building from 1958 that nobody has ever had the money to ruin. Out front, on a pole taller than the building, a neon star with five points, two of them dead, so that from the highway it looks like a star that lost a fight and stayed open anyway.

Inside there’s a coffee counter with stools bolted to the floor and boomerangs in the Formica, a rack of cassettes and beef jerky by the register, a hand-lettered card taped to the cash drawer — SHOWERS · DRIVERS · $8 · ASK — and through an archway a back room of red leatherette booths, patched here and there with red tape. Four men sit along the counter in caps and canvas coats that have done more work than the Carhartt ever will, each with his own sugar pourer and his own silence. The night waitress wears BEV on her name tag and is somewhere in her sixties, with her hair up in a clip and a pencil stuck through it. She takes in the two of them — a barefoot girl, and a boy carrying a pie into a place that sells pie — and says, “You kids sit anywhere,” and means the back.

There’s a jukebox in the archway, a Seeburg with its chrome gone milky. Skye feeds it a quarter before she does anything else and punches in a number without bothering with the cards, and by the time they’re sliding into a booth by the window, Mazzy Star is coming out of it slow and underwater: a slide guitar, a tambourine somebody is barely touching, and a girl singing from the bottom of a well.

She takes the side facing the archway. He takes the window, and sets Gloria’s box against the wall beside the napkins. Bev comes with two heavy cups and a pot. “Two lemon meringue,” Skye tells her, “and coffee till we die. He’s paying.” Bev writes it down without comment and goes.

Within ten minutes Skye’s bare feet are up on his side of the booth, crossed at the ankle on the red leatherette by his hip, braided anklet and all. She came in off forty degrees of gravel with nothing on them. He touches the top of one with the back of his hand, to check, and it’s warm. The cold doesn’t seem to apply to her.

body.text: “How’s Marlene?” she asks, with a look at his eyebrow, once Bev is out of earshot. “Still in Erie,” he says. “He took her back.” “I’m still not buying it,” Skye says, and goes on with her coffee as if she has all the time in the world to wait for the real one.

body: The pie comes, two tall slices with the meringue browned into peaks. She picks up her fork, and before the first bite she looks once out the window beside him — at the black glass, the gravel, the trucks asleep in their rows under the lamps — and then she eats like she hasn’t since Sunday.

At the counter a minivan family is refueling on the way to somebody’s Thanksgiving: a father asleep sitting up with his cap over his eyes, a mother doing math on a napkin, a little boy under the stools, and a girl of about thirteen in pajama pants and a Hollister hoodie, who swivels around on her stool and stares into the back room with her mouth open. She tugs her mother’s sleeve and whispers. Her mother doesn’t look up from the napkin. Skye, still chewing, gives the girl a small wave with the fork hand, and the girl ducks behind her mother like she’s been shot at. Jack figures nobody ever told the kid you’re allowed to eat pie barefoot at half past one in the morning, and here’s the proof.
“So what was it?” he says. It’s a fair question; he’s been carrying it since Sunday. “The job.”
“A carpet,” she says. “A wall. A woman with pins in her mouth.”
“That’s three jobs.”
“It’s one job with three kinds of standing still.”
“Okay. What are you *in*?”

She looks at him over the heavy cup, taking her time about it, and he can see she’s enjoying this. Then she pulls a napkin out of the dispenser, takes a Sharpie out of the flannel’s pocket, uncaps it with her teeth, writes on the napkin in capitals, and turns it around and slides it across the table.

“I kept reading,” she says. “After Friday. ‘Good Country People’ is in the same book, a couple of stories on. Hulga. Thirty-two years old, a PhD in philosophy and a wooden leg, and she thinks she’s smarter than God.”
“So she’s me.”
“So she’s *me*.” She taps the napkin with the Sharpie. “You’re the Bible salesman. Go.”
“I don’t —”
“You do one voice. I was there. Tonight you do two.” She pushes Gloria’s box across the table at him, string and all. “That’s your sample case.”
Mazzy Star goes on being underwater. Skye folds her hands on the Formica, a philosopher with a wooden leg and no time for salesmen, and waits for hers.

choices.text: Commit — the full Tennessee pitch, hat in hand.
choices.key: At the Starlite she cast you as O’Connor’s Bible salesman, and you committed.
response: He stands up. That’s the first thing — he gets up out of the booth of a truck stop on the 101 and takes off a hat he isn’t wearing and holds it over his heart, and lifts Gloria’s box by the string like a valise full of Scripture, and what comes out of his mouth is from three states south of anywhere he has ever been. He’s just a country boy, ma’am. He’s selling Bibles. He could tell from the road she was real good country people, and he’s come to speak of serious things. He sits down on the edge of her side of the booth, uninvited. He calls her ma’am eleven times. He turns the hat around and around by its brim.

He’s good. Neither of them saw it coming, him least of all, and for most of a minute he forgets to be embarrassed. Hulga runs out of lines before he does. Skye sits there with her mouth a little open, and then she says, as nobody but herself, “There’s a second voice in there. I *knew* it.”

Then she’s somebody else again: a man at the back of a soundstage with a headset clamped over one ear and a coffee gone cold, who has seen everything twice and would like to see his kids. She presses a finger to the headset that isn’t there. “Moving on,” she tells a booth Jack can’t see. Then, to Jack, flat as a man who has said it four thousand times: “You’re cast.”

She never does say what she’s in. By the time that occurs to him she’s on to the Saab: when did he hear? Before her, it turns out — Rudy’s radio, KNX, at twenty to ten, twelve minutes ahead of her text. “You could have warned me,” she says, and lifts her heavy cup toward the window, where the Saab sits under a lamp with its top up against the cold. “To the orphan.” He touches his cup to hers.

choices.text: Play him from Youngstown. “Bibles. Hollow. There’s Marlboros in ’em.”
choices.key: At the Starlite she cast you as O’Connor’s Bible salesman; you played him from Youngstown.
response: He doesn’t go south. He stays right where he is, in Mahoning County, and leans across the table, low and confidential, Southern Park Mall parking lot after dark. “Bibles,” he says, low. “Good ones. King James, leather, the works.” He taps the lid of the box. “Hollow. There’s a carton of Marlboros in there and a deck of cards. You want ’em, you want ’em. I ain’t standing here all night.”
“Twenty bucks,” Hulga says, rallying, “and I’ll throw in the leg.”
She breaks first. She drops Hulga in the middle of a word and laughs at the ceiling with her mouth wide open, and she doesn’t do a thing to hide it.

choices.text: “I do one.” Make her play both.
choices.key: At the Starlite she cast you as O’Connor’s Bible salesman. You made her play both parts.
response: “I do one,” he says, and sits back against the leatherette. “You do both.”

She narrows her eyes at him, and then she does. She’s Hulga, dry as a blackboard, a philosopher in a sweatshirt who wouldn’t be caught dead being charmed; then she slides down the bench and she’s the salesman, hat in her hands and *ma’am* in every sentence; then she’s back, arguing with herself across the napkin dispenser, and Hulga is losing and knows it and hates it. Then she stops, and holds the Sharpie out across the table at him like a microphone.
“One line,” she says. “Yours. In your own voice.”
“Which one?”
“His last. In the barn, when he’s got her leg in his valise.”
He thinks about it. Then he gives it to her in the voice he was born with, Glenwood Avenue, no South in it anywhere: “You ain’t so smart.”
She sits back and looks at him. It’s the best line in the scene, and they both know it.

choices.text: “Yes, and —” Recast her as the salesman, yourself as Hulga’s mother.
choices.key: At the Starlite she cast you as O’Connor’s Bible salesman. You recast the scene.
response: “Yes, and,” Jack says. “You’re the salesman. I’m her mother.”
“You don’t get to recast my —”

But he already has. He folds his hands on the Formica and becomes Mrs. Hopewell in her kitchen, beaming over the lemon meringue at a Bible salesman she has no intention of buying from. He tells the salesman nothing is perfect. He tells him that is life. He tells him other people have their opinions too. He invites him to supper, and then to stay for pie, and then to go and see the barn, and keeps on inviting him until the salesman runs out of ways to say no — Skye, as the salesman, is laughing too hard to say much of anything — and then he waves the scene off down the road and straight into the ditch, on purpose.
She stops playing to watch him do it. “You *improv*,” she says. “Who taught you?”
“My sister. The supper table.”

body: By five past two the minivan family has paid and gone. Crossing the gravel, the girl in pajama pants walks backward to the van so she can keep looking at the window, and her mother steers her by the hood. Bev comes through the archway with the pot, tops up both their cups, and goes back to her truckers.
“You know,” Jack says, “if you ever get on TV, I’ll buy one. Just to watch.”

Skye laughs into her coffee. It goes everywhere — the cup, the saucer, the front of the flannel — and the trucker nearest the archway turns around on his stool to see what happened back there. She waves a napkin at him: nothing, sorry, carry on. “Deal,” she says, mopping. “*Deal*.” She doesn’t explain. Jack decides it’s two in the morning, and at two in the morning everything is a little funny.
She nods at the box against the wall. “Tell me about the pie.”
“It isn’t mine. It’s for my grandmother.” He turns his cup around by the handle. “She fell on Monday.”
She stops eating to listen, and he tells her.

choices.text: All of it — the stairs she’d been keeping off, the wrist, the stitches, the monitor, the ride.
response: He tells her all of it. The Hollis steps, and Gina’s text with no capitals and no punctuation and the word *ambulance* in the middle of it. The stairs his grandmother had been keeping off all fall, sleeping in her chair in the front room so she wouldn’t have to climb them, and went up on Monday anyway, nobody knows why, and came down. His sister finding her. St. Elizabeth’s. A broken wrist, six stitches over the eye, and a monitor on her heart because of the dizzy spells; they’re keeping her for that.
“And my dad drove her.” She hears that, and that’s all he gives her of it.
She listens the way she listened in the car on Friday, chin down, all of her pointed at it, and when he runs out she reaches across and takes a swallow of his coffee instead of saying anything.

choices.text: The facts, flat.
response: He gives it to her the way his mother gave it to him on the stairwell on Monday: St. Elizabeth’s. A broken wrist. Six stitches. A monitor for her heart. Stable. He leaves out the chair, and the stairs, and who drove.
Skye takes the facts one at a time and sets them out on the table in front of her like she’s going to need them later.

choices.text: “She called the paramedic handsome. Twice. She’s eighty-four. She’s fine.”
response: “She called the paramedic handsome,” Jack says. “Twice. She’s eighty-four. She’s fine.”
Skye looks at him over the coffee.
“Okay,” she says. “Now tell me the real one.”
And he does, some of it: the stairs she’d been keeping off all fall, sleeping in her chair in the front room, and went up anyway; the wrist; the monitor on her heart.

body: “Tell me about her,” Skye says. “Not the fall. *Her*.”

She leans in on her elbows with the fork still in her hand and turns every bit of herself toward him, and it’s the window seat again: the feeling of the lights in a room being adjusted, one at a time, until the only one left on is the one on him.

So he tells her. Carmela Rinaldi, eighty-four, from San Giovanni in Fiore, up in the mountains in Calabria, where the winters are worse than Youngstown’s — she says it like a boast. Came over in 1951 with one suitcase. The rosary every night in Calabrese, which is not Italian, she’ll tell you, and which the saints understand better. Cardoons at every holiday, battered and fried, which nobody in the house likes and everybody eats. A twenty folded small and pressed into his palm at the door every time he leaves, with a look that means don’t tell your mother. The chair by the front window, where she says the beads and keeps an eye on Glenwood Avenue to see who isn’t going to Mass.
“She calls me Giacomino,” he says. “And every phone call, she asks the same thing. *E la ragazza?*”
“What’s that?”
“‘And the girl?’”
“Which girl?”
He picks up his coffee.

body.text: Skye watches him drink it. “Right,” she says. “The one who’s seeing somebody.” She doesn’t make it a question, and she moves on without a ripple: what is a cardoon, actually, botanically, because she has been nodding at the word for five minutes and has no idea. A thistle, he tells her. You eat the stalks. She looks at him as if he has confessed to a crime in a foreign country and she’d like to visit.

body: “I could do her,” she says. “Give me a line. How does she say *ragazza*?” And she has already started — the shoulders coming down and in, one hand going up to settle a kerchief that isn’t there, the chin lifting toward a window on a street she has never seen —
Then she sets her fork down on the plate.
“No,” she says. “I’m not doing her. She’s yours.”
She turns the fork over, tines down, and looks at it.
“I’m named for a grandmother I met twice,” she says. “She sent me a holy card every birthday till I was nine. Saints. Gold around the edges. I don’t have any of them.”
Then she picks the fork back up, takes the last of the meringue off his plate with it, and she’s back. “When do you go?”
“Today. In about five hours. With my roommate.”
“Good,” she says, as if that settles the roommate, and goes straight on. “Five hours. Give me Thanksgiving. Give me the table. Who sits where.”

He gives her the table on Glenwood Avenue: his father at the end by the kitchen door, his mother never sitting down, Nonna at the corner where she can reach everything and correct everyone, his sisters, and this year an extra chair. She wants to know what’s on it. She wants to know who carves. She wants to know if anybody cries, and when he says his mother, at grace, every year, she nods like that was the right answer.
“What about you?”

“My mother’s,” Skye says. “There’ll be a lot of people I don’t know, and all of them will be very interested in how I’m doing.” She smiles when she says it, a smile with a good many teeth in it, and pours more sugar into a coffee that already has plenty.
At five to three Bev comes around again with the pot, and this time she stops with it over Skye’s cup and doesn’t pour. She studies Skye over the top of her reading glasses.
“Anybody ever tell you you look like somebody?”
“Everybody looks like somebody, Bev,” Skye says, sweet as anything.
Bev weighs that, pours, and takes the pot back up front.
It’s a good line. Jack would like to have it.
Skye watches her go. Then she wraps both hands around the heavy cup and looks at him across the table, and she’s quieter than she’s been all night.
“Can I ask you something?”
“You’ve been asking me things for an hour and a half.”
“Something I want to know.” She works out how to put it. “Not the argument. I can do the argument — you did it in the window on Friday, it was very good. What’s it *like*? Believing. On a Tuesday.”
He opens his mouth and doesn’t have it ready.

“I do yoga,” she says, to help. “There’s a part at the end, savasana — you lie on your back on the floor with your palms up like you’re dead, it’s actually called corpse pose — and the teacher walks around in her socks and says, *You are exactly where you need to be.* And every single time, for about one breath, I believe her.” She thinks about it. “Then I think about my car.”
“Corpse pose,” Jack says, delighted.

“It’s very restful. And the philosophy part I get. The First Mover. Somebody had to start it, something can’t come out of nothing — that’s a plot problem, and somebody has to solve it. That’s just a good writers’ room.”

body.text: She tips her head at him. “On the beach you said most nights nobody answers, and you go anyway.” She turns the cup a quarter turn on its saucer. “I keep thinking about that. It’s a terrible business plan.”

body: “On a Tuesday,” Jack says, slowly, because he wants to get it right for her, “mostly it’s a Hail Mary in the shower when I can’t think —”
“Hail Mary, full of grace,” Skye says.

He stops. She doesn’t — “the Lord is with thee” — and he goes with her, because he can’t not; he has been saying it with whoever starts it since before he could tie his shoes. So they say the first half together across a booth in a truck stop at three in the morning, low, under the jukebox: *Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.* She has every word, and every word in its place, and every one of them a little careful, set down by itself, none of the run-together of a kid who learned it kneeling at a wake. She stops at the Holy Name like it’s the end of her line.
“For a role,” she says. “Forty takes. A chapel.”
“What were you playing?”
“A nice girl.”

He laughs. She is so pleased with herself for knowing it, and she is so close — she has the words, every one, better than half the Newman Center — and he wants to give her the rest of it, the half that asks for something, *now and at the hour of our death*, and he doesn’t know how you hand that to somebody across a table. He turns his cup around by the handle and doesn’t drink from it. Under the table her bare feet find his shin and settle there, and she waits for him to tell her what it’s like.

choices.text: “Like being known. All of it, even the parts you’d cut — and not getting thrown out.”
choices.key: At the Starlite Skye asked what believing is like. You said: like being known, and not getting thrown out.
response: “Like being known,” Jack says. “All of it. Even the parts you’d cut. And not getting thrown out.”
She takes that in slowly, her thumb going around the rim of the cup.
Then her face clears. She has found the door, and she’s pleased, and she means every word of what comes next. “So it’s like acting,” she says. “You do it long enough, and it becomes true.”
“It’s the other way round,” Jack says. “It’s true first.”
“Is it?”

She isn’t arguing. She wants to know; she leans across the table to hear it. And he has a hundred ways to say it — Aquinas, Augustine, Newman, Nonna’s beads going through her fingers in the chair by the window — and not one of them will go across a booth. He holds the heavy cup in both hands. Her feet are warm against his shin. Out on the gravel the first of the trucks starts up, deep in its chest, and then another.
“Yeah,” he says. “It is.”
She nods slowly, keeping it, a line she means to understand later.

body: A trucker feeds a dollar into the jukebox on his way down the hall to the showers, a towel over his shoulder and a shaving kit under his arm, and he’s gone before his song comes on. It plays for the two of them instead: Merle Haggard, “Silver Wings,” a steel guitar and a man standing on a runway watching somebody leave.
“How are you getting home?” Skye says.
“Plane. One change. My dad’s meeting us in Pittsburgh.” He hears himself add the next part. “I’ve never been up.”
She stops with the cup halfway to her mouth. “Never?”
“My dad drove me out in August. In the truck.”
She puts the cup down. “Get the window,” she says. “Don’t blink. You only get the first one once.”
“That’s the advice?”
“That’s all of it. What do you do up there — do you pray?”
“I’ll pray.”
“For what?”
“That it stays up.”
“That’s just physics.”
“Then I’ll pray for physics.”
She laughs, and then she folds her hands around the cup on the table, and he watches her decide something.

“I want you to miss me,” she says. “Over Thanksgiving. A reasonable amount.” She says it the way she ordered the pie, as a thing a person might simply want and ask for, in a public place, with truckers. “Is that allowed?”
On Glenwood Avenue people want things for twenty years and die without mentioning it. She has mentioned it over lemon meringue at half past three in the morning, and now she is waiting to hear back.

It’s easier to say than he would have bet, and he doesn’t take any of it back.
Skye goes quiet. She looks pleased, and a little surprised to be pleased. “Good,” she says. “I’ll know if you don’t.”

body: She drives him back down the grade with the heater on and the tape turned low, and they don’t talk. He doesn’t want to, and she seems to have decided not to, and the twenty minutes are better for it.

The Anacapa lot at a quarter past four is dew on windshields and sodium light, and one of the lamps on the Lagoon side has a tick in it, a dry click every few seconds, like it’s keeping time for somebody. The moon went down hours ago. She pulls into the far row by the bike racks and turns the engine off, and the tape stops in the middle of a word.
In the quiet she turns in her seat to face him, one bare foot tucked up under her.

body.text: “I’m not going to ask this time,” she says. “Last time you didn’t let me get to the end of the sentence.”
body.else: “I’m not going to ask this time,” she says.

body: “And I’m not doing the grandmother tonight. I retired her.”

Then she waits. She’s good at it. She waits with all of herself, as though the lamps and the cars and the eucalyptus have been switched off and there’s nothing left in the world for her to look at but him.

She makes a small surprised sound against his mouth — the first thing all night he has gotten past her — and then she kisses him back, hard, and then she takes her mouth away just far enough to talk.
“Out,” she says. “Properly.” She opens her door.

Then she sighs, enormously. “You’re very slow, Ohio,” she says. “I’m going to have to do everything.” She leans across the gearshift and kisses him once, quick, to show him how it’s done, and opens her door. “Out. I’m saying goodbye properly.”

s20k.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:20 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT, AGAINST THE SAAB
body: When he gets around the back of the car she’s leaning on the driver’s door in the green flannel with her bare feet on the cold asphalt and her hands in her pockets, waiting for him like there is no plane in the morning and never will be.
“Slow,” she says. “Friday was fast. I want to see what you’re like slow.”
He comes in close enough that she has to tip her head back to look at him. She doesn’t take her hands out of her pockets. She makes him come the rest of the way.

For the first second her mouth is cool from the air, and still. She doesn’t do anything with it, and neither does he. They stand in the orange light with their mouths just touching, and he can feel her breathing, and the cold, and his own heart going in his ears. Then she opens her mouth under his, slowly, and it starts.

She tastes of coffee and the lemon off the pie — on Friday it was salt — and she kisses the way she said she would, slow on purpose, every second of it something she has decided. When he goes faster she goes slower and makes him come back down to her. Her hands come out of the flannel and go inside his open Carhartt and lie flat against his shirt, over his ribs, warm through the cotton, and they stay there while his heart knocks against one of them.

He gets a hand into her hair. It’s dry tonight, and heavy, and it slides through his fingers and falls back against her neck, and he follows it down to the hinge of her jaw and holds her face there with his thumb along her cheekbone. Her jaw fits his palm like it was measured for it. He kisses the corner of her mouth, and then the place his thumb was, and then lower, the side of her throat where her pulse is going, and she tips her head back against the cold canvas of the top to give it to him and says something that isn’t a word. He comes back up to her mouth and she’s already there, open, waiting for him.

She takes him by the front of the Carhartt and pulls, and keeps on pulling, until there’s no air left anywhere along him that isn’t her — the door at her back, her hips against his, her knees, the cold flannel and the warm girl inside it. He is eighteen and he has wanted this since she put her feet up on his side of the booth, and his body is completely honest about it. Pressed against him like this she can’t help knowing. She doesn’t move away. She makes a low pleased sound into his mouth instead, and he feels it in the backs of his knees.

The cold is everywhere they aren’t touching: the back of his neck, the backs of his hands, his ears, his ankles where his jeans ride up. Everywhere they are, it’s gone. The lamp ticks over them. He stops counting the ticks; he stops knowing how long. A car goes by out on Ocean Road and its headlights swing across the two of them and keep going, and he doesn’t stop for it, and she doesn’t either.

Some part of him is keeping very exact track of his hands. One is in her hair. The other is open on the flannel at the small of her back, where the shirt has ridden up over her cutoffs and there’s a strip of her, bare and warm, that he can feel the heat of without touching. He keeps his hand on the flannel. He knows exactly where it is, and exactly where it isn’t, and why, the way you know where the edge of a roof is in the dark.

She feels him keep it there. He can tell, because she smiles against his mouth — the corner of her top lip going up under his — and kisses him harder, slow and harder, like she has found a game she likes and means to play it for a long time.
Somewhere in it she says his name, once, against his jaw, and then she goes back to his mouth, and he forgets to answer.
The lamp ticks. Her hands have closed in his shirt. She isn’t going to be the one, not yet; he can tell by how she’s holding on.

body: He’s the one who stops. He takes his mouth off hers and steps back half a step, not far; his forehead stays against hers, and both of them are breathing like they ran up the grade. Her hands are still inside his jacket.

She opens her eyes and looks at him from very close. She looks interested, and pleased, the way she looked at him across the napkin at the Starlite — like she has just watched him do a thing she wasn’t sure he could do, and liked the way he did it.
“Go home, Ohio,” she says. “You have a plane.”
She takes her hands back out of his Carhartt one at a time, and does up the top snap for him against the cold, and gets in. The window comes down a crack.
“Miss me a reasonable amount.”

Then the Saab backs out of the row and crosses the lot, the one taillight swinging red across the wet asphalt, and turns onto Ocean Road toward the 101 and Los Angeles. He stands where she left him until he can’t hear the engine anymore.
She’s the one. She takes her mouth away, and when he leans after it she puts her thumb on his mouth, where hers was, and holds it there.

He stands still for it. Her thumb is warm and a little rough at the edge of the nail, and she keeps it on his lower lip while she looks at him, like she wants to remember exactly where she left off. Then she steps back with her thumb still up between them, as if she could hold the place.
“That’s for the plane,” she says.
She gets in. The window comes down a crack.
“Miss me a reasonable amount.”

Then the Saab backs out of the row and crosses the lot, the one taillight swinging red across the wet asphalt, and turns onto Ocean Road toward the 101. He stands where she left him until he can’t hear the engine anymore.

s21.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:40 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT, THE CURB BY THE BIKE RACKS → ROOM 412
body: He sits down on the curb by the bike racks because his legs make a good case for it, with Gloria’s box on his knees. It’s twenty to five. The lot is dew and orange light, the eucalyptus along the Lagoon black against a sky that hasn’t started anything yet, and he sits there for forty minutes, and all forty of them are her mouth.

He goes through it from the beginning. The first second, before either of them moved: her mouth against his, cool from the air, not doing anything, and her breath going in and out against his upper lip. After that, the coffee and the lemon. The chapped place low on her lip, on the left, from the cold or from driving the 101 all fall with the top down — the one rough thing about her; he found it and she made a sound in her throat and didn’t mind. The freckle at the corner of her mouth that he found before he ever saw it. The bow of her top lip, which comes to a small peak in the middle, like somebody drew it there to show you where to start.

The way that lip lifted when she smiled into it, so that he felt the smile before he could see anything — felt it go up against his mouth at the corner and knew she was pleased with him. How slow she was. How she would draw back until their mouths were barely touching, and wait there, and make him come the rest of the way, every time. That she meant it. That it was on purpose. That she’d been thinking about it since Friday, and told him so.

body.text: He gets to the end — his forehead against hers, both of them breathing hard, *Go home, Ohio* — and goes back to the first second.
body.else: He gets to the end — her thumb on his mouth, where hers had been — and goes back to the first second.

body: At some point he has the RAZR out. It’s open in his hand to SKYE (MISFIT), and his thumb is resting on the 5. He doesn’t press it. He closes the phone and holds it.
At some point his other hand has gone up to the St. Michael at his throat. It’s warm from him. He keeps hold of it.

He knows how it would go in the box on a Saturday — *Bless me, Father* — and the sentence after that, which would have her in it, and *four days*, and *I wanted* — and he lets the sentence stop there, because he isn’t in the box. He’s on a curb with a pie. Her mouth is still on his, more or less. He can feel exactly where.
At ten past five the sprinklers along the Lagoon path come on all at once, hissing, and one of them gets the curb. He takes the hint.

In 412 Theo is sitting up in bed in the navy robe with his iPhone in his lap and an alarm set for half past that he isn’t going to need. He watches Jack come in and sit down on his own bed in the Carhartt with the pie box on his knees, and he looks confused again, the way he looked at six on Saturday, with something under the confusion that is starting to take notes.
“Did you sleep?”
“No.”
“Doing what?” Theo says. “Another book?”

journal.title: Skye
journal.text: Skye. No last name — she said *Out*. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Doesn’t go here. Not yet, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Named for a grandmother she met twice. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose.

Theo looks at the duffel on the floor at the foot of Jack’s bed, unzipped and empty, with one sock in it.
“Of course,” Theo says, and lies back down in the robe, and looks at the ceiling with great interest.

“About?”
Jack looks down at the box on his knees. “Pie.”
It’s nearly true. Theo studies him from the pillow with the face he keeps for subtitles, and then reaches over and turns off the alarm he wasn’t going to need.

“You weren’t using it.”
Theo opens his mouth, and closes it, and lies back down in the robe with an arm over his eyes. “I hate that you’re funny at five in the morning,” he says, from under the arm.
